title: Earthworms and soil health: what worms do for soil and how farmers count them with a shovel

sources.title: Willamette Valley Soil Quality Card Guide (EM 8710), section 5: Are earthworms abundant in the soil?
sources.note: 只取事實；與 USDA NRCS 合編，給農民在田裡自行評估土壤

sources.publisher: Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO)
sources.title: Plant Production and Protection Division: Earthworms (soil biodiversity)

facts.text: A simple field test is to dig out one shovelful of topsoil at least 6 inches (about 15 cm) deep and carefully count the earthworms in it.
In the Oregon guide, more than five earthworms in a shovelful of topsoil is the preferred result, about three is moderate, and none at all is the least desirable.
The guide says to count earthworms in late spring and late fall, when the soil is moist but not soaked and fairly warm.
If the topsoil is too dry or too wet, or too hot or too cold, earthworms may not be seen even in healthy soil.
Earthworms are most active in spring and autumn.
Water makes up more than 75% of an earthworm's body weight, so earthworms prefer moist soil.
A count of 100 earthworms per square meter in a farm field is considered good.
Surface-feeding earthworms eat plant litter such as dead leaves, and some kinds pull plant material from the surface down into their burrows.
Earthworm casts, the waste they leave behind, contain more bacteria, organic matter, and plant nutrients than the soil around them.
Earthworm burrows let more air and water into the soil, improve drainage, and make it easier for roots to grow; roots often follow old burrows.
Slime from earthworms binds soil particles together into stable crumbs.
Earthworms are called ecosystem engineers because their feeding and digging strongly change the soil, plant growth, and the cycling of nutrients.
Plowing destroys burrows and removes the plant material on the surface that feeds and shelters earthworms.
In fields that are not plowed (no-till), earthworm numbers can reach two to three times those in plowed fields.
Some insecticides, fungicides, and ammonia-based fertilizers harm earthworms.
Few or no earthworms is a sign that the soil has little plant matter in it or is too hot and dry, conditions that are also bad for crops.
There are more than 3,000 kinds of earthworms; farm soils may hold 30 to 300 earthworms per square meter.
Some earthworms dig vertical burrows at least 3 meters deep.
